title: Jaishankar Says India Has Gone 'Beyond Advocacy' in Russia-Ukraine Conflict
excerpt: At the Munich Leaders Meeting, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said New Delhi is now holding direct talks with both Moscow and Kyiv on Black Sea shipping, grain and energy exports, and 'non-attack possibilities'.
body:
• External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar told the Munich Leaders Meeting that India has "got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy" on the Russia-Ukraine conflict in recent months, holding direct conversations with both Moscow and Kyiv.
  • The talks are practical, not grand peace summits: Black Sea shipping safety, grain exports, energy exports, and "non-attack possibilities" — issues where both sides have immediate concerns.
  • Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called India's plan "the most comprehensive" of four peace proposals Kyiv is reviewing, alongside submissions from Turkey, Egypt, and the United States.
  • Russian President Vladimir Putin separately praised Prime Minister Narendra Modi's "good ideas" for ending the war, saying Modi raises the issue at every bilateral meeting.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said on Sunday that India has moved from urging diplomacy to actively facilitating arrangements between Russia and Ukraine, the clearest public signal yet that New Delhi is prepared to play a hands-on role in the conflict's resolution.

Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting, Jaishankar said India's position on the war has long been consistent — that the conflict must end through dialogue and diplomacy — but that its engagement has deepened in recent months.

"We have been advocating it for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy. We have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard."

— S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister

From advocacy to operational engagement

Jaishankar sketched the contours of India's current involvement: conversations with both warring parties aimed at resolving immediate operational concerns. "We are trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue, but going beyond that to cover some immediate concerns which both of them have on grain exports, energy exports, non-attack possibilities," he said. "Those are ongoing conversations right now."

The framing matters. New Delhi is not claiming a mediation mandate or hosting a peace conference. Instead, it is positioning itself as a trusted channel on the practical arrangements — shipping corridors, energy flows, agricultural exports — that any eventual ceasefire would need to sustain. It is the same sequencing India used in its shuttle engagement of recent years, when National Security Adviser Ajit Doval visited both Moscow and Kyiv and Prime Minister Modi travelled to both capitals.

The remarks followed a meeting of the Consultative Committee of the Ministry of External Affairs on India-Russia relations on October 3, where members reviewed New Delhi's active engagements with both Moscow and Kyiv to help end hostilities, along with progress on transit projects, energy cooperation, and strategic connectivity.

Both sides are publicly validating India's role

The clearest external validation came from Kyiv. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine is reviewing four international peace proposals — from India, Turkey, Egypt, and the United States — and described India's as "the most comprehensive." "For the first time, India has signalled its willingness to play a role," Sybiha said at a press briefing, as reported by RBC-Ukraine.

Moscow, for its part, has been equally warm. Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow that Modi consistently raises the war at every bilateral meeting and has offered "very good ideas" for a mutually acceptable solution. Putin said he felt it his "duty" to state this openly and expressed gratitude for Modi's commitment to a peaceful resolution.

The endorsement from both sides is the crux of India's proposition. Few capitals maintain working relationships with both Moscow and Kyiv of sufficient depth to pass messages; India, which has refused to condemn Russia while buying discounted crude and simultaneously hosting Ukrainian leadership, is one of them.

Why the Russia relationship still matters to India

Jaishankar anchored the diplomacy in history, recalling the Soviet Union's backing of India "when our security, when our territorial integrity was under threat" and "when much of the world preferred backing a military regime next to us." "India and Russia have historically had very good relations, particularly since the 1950s. That history is not forgotten," he said.

But he stressed that the relationship has outgrown its Cold War security roots. "Today, the relationship has widened beyond that. It is very much more today an economic relationship as well," he said, pointing to military, nuclear, and space cooperation alongside a significant volume of trade, investment, energy, and resources. India's stated energy objective remains safeguarding Indian consumers — a reference to the discounted Russian crude imports that have helped moderate domestic fuel prices since 2022, even as Western sanctions reshaped global energy flows.

What it means for the diaspora

For Indians abroad, the remarks are a signal of the government's confidence in New Delhi's diplomatic standing. India's ability to speak with both sides underpins not just peace prospects but the practical corridors — shipping, energy, grain — that affect commodity prices and supply chains touching diaspora businesses and household budgets alike.

What to watch

The next round of India-Russia bilateral consultations and any follow-up diplomatic contacts will be scrutinised for signs of progress. The real test of the "beyond advocacy" posture is whether the Black Sea and energy conversations produce tangible arrangements — or stall the way earlier peace proposals have. Either way, Jaishankar has set the marker: India no longer wants to be counted only as a voice urging negotiations. It wants to be at the table arranging them.
